The note leaves the induction open. Its concrete starting idea is to bound recurrence coefficients, then use their product to control a finite approximation to \(H_\lambda\). Your proposal adds another step: proving a zero statement that survives as the approximation covers larger heights. I’m checking how those two steps could fit together.

The existing bounds already support the approximation side of your idea: increasing the degree lets us control larger real-height windows. The part still to find is an induction that controls zeros. Real roots of \(P_N(u)\) do not imply real zeros of the finite Fourier approximation; even Gaussian quadrature gives a simple example of that distinction.

A useful distinction is emerging: an induction could carry coefficient bounds, a controlled replacement for the omitted tail, or a certificate about zeros in a growing region. I’ll spell out what each would need to carry from one degree to the next, and save the discussion as an exploratory note so we can continue from it.

Your understanding is essentially correct. **Your truncation proposal could fit into a proof by induction:** construct increasingly accurate finite approximations, prove an appropriate statement about their zeros, and pass to the limit. The brainstorm’s concrete suggestion develops the approximation side. Your proposal asks how to add the zero-control side.

Let me clarify the representation first, then distinguish the possible inductions.

The \(P_n(u;\lambda)\) are monic orthogonal polynomials for \(W_\lambda(u)\,du\). More precisely, \(h_n\) is their **squared norm**, so
\[
p_n=\frac{P_n}{\sqrt{h_n}},
\qquad
\beta_n=\frac{h_n}{h_{n-1}},
\qquad
a_n=\sqrt{\beta_n}.
\]
Multiplication by \(u\) has the recurrence
\[
uP_n=P_{n+1}+\beta_nP_{n-1}.
\]
In the orthonormal basis, its matrix is \(J\), with \(a_n\) connecting positions \(n-1\) and \(n\).

Your interpretation of the exponential is right: multiplication by \(e^{ixu}\) becomes the operator \(e^{ixJ}\). If
\[
d\mu_\lambda=\frac{W_\lambda(u)\,du}{Z_\lambda},
\qquad
F_\lambda(z)=\frac{2H_\lambda(z)}{Z_\lambda},
\]
then
\[
F_\lambda(x)=\langle e_0,e^{ixJ(\lambda)}e_0\rangle.
\]
Here \(e_0\) represents the constant polynomial. We are extracting one scalar entry of the exponential of the multiplication operator.

Changing \(\lambda\) changes the weight and therefore the orthogonal basis and its coefficients:
\[
\partial_\lambda\beta_n
=\beta_n(\beta_{n+1}-\beta_{n-1}),
\qquad
\partial_\lambda a_n
=\frac{a_n}{2}(\beta_{n+1}-\beta_{n-1}).
\]
This describes the same deformation for which
\[
\partial_\lambda H_\lambda=-\partial_z^2H_\lambda.
\]
Alternatively, we can keep the basis at \(\lambda=1/2\) fixed and insert the factor \(e^{-\tau J_*^2}\), where \(\tau=1/2-\lambda\). Those are two ways of organizing the same flow.

One adjustment matters for your truncation idea: **the \(P_n\) form a basis, but we do not yet have a useful series \(H=\sum_n P_n\).** If we expand \(e^{izu}\) in that basis, its coefficient along the constant polynomial is already \(F_\lambda(z)\). Simply truncating that exact expansion would therefore presuppose the quantity we want to compute. Truncating the matrix evolution gives a constructive version of your idea.

**The concrete idea in the brainstorm is to propagate useful coefficient information into an approximation bound.** Its structure is
\[
\text{source information}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\text{bounds on }\beta_n
\;\longrightarrow\;
\frac{h_N}{h_0}=\prod_{j=1}^{N}\beta_j
\;\longrightarrow\;
\text{error in approximating }H_\lambda.
\]

For example, if we can prove \(\beta_{n+1}\le B_n\), then
\[
\frac{h_{n+1}}{h_0}
=\beta_{n+1}\frac{h_n}{h_0}
\le B_n\frac{h_n}{h_0}.
\]
That is an elementary induction on the norm product. The interesting question is whether a stronger collection of inequalities can itself be propagated from one degree to the next.

The Volterra equation exposes the difficulty:
\[
\beta_{n+1}
=\beta_{n-1}+\partial_\lambda\log\beta_n.
\]
Knowing a bound on \(\beta_n\) does not automatically bound its derivative. Thus “assume the first \(n\) coefficients are bounded” is generally too weak an inductive hypothesis. We might need to carry derivative bounds, relations between neighboring coefficients, or auxiliary source integrals.

The source-dependent identity highlighted in the brainstorm is
\[
\int V_\lambda'(u)P_n(u)P_{n-1}(u)W_\lambda(u)\,du
=n h_{n-1},
\qquad V_\lambda=-\log W_\lambda.
\]
It follows from integration by parts and orthogonality. For a Gaussian, \(V'\) is linear and this immediately gives \(\beta_n=n\sigma^2\). For a quartic weight, \(V'\) is cubic and produces a relation involving only neighboring coefficients. This is a concrete illustration of how the source can supply a closed relation in degree. The theta source has not yet yielded such a closure. [Van Assche, §3](https://arxiv.org/html/2202.11017v1#S3)

The existing logarithmic coefficient bound was proved using confinement at every degree; the note does **not** already contain a nontrivial coefficient induction that proves a statement about zeros.

**Your truncation idea has a particularly natural realization here.** Keep the first \(N\) basis positions and let \(J_N\) be the resulting finite matrix. Define
\[
F_{\lambda,N}(z)=\langle e_0,e^{izJ_N}e_0\rangle.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
F_{\lambda,N}(z)=\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{j,N}e^{izu_{j,N}},
\]
where the \(u_{j,N}\) are the roots of \(P_N\) and the weights are positive. This is Gaussian quadrature for the source measure. It matches the source moments through degree \(2N-1\). [NIST’s quadrature description](https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.5#v)

There is a useful chain explanation: starting at position zero, a walk needs at least \(2N\) steps to cross the omitted boundary and return. Consequently,
\[
\langle e_0,J^ke_0\rangle
=\langle e_0,J_N^ke_0\rangle
\qquad(k<2N).
\]
So the Taylor expansions of the two Fourier observations agree through that order. This makes your Taylor-series analogy quite precise.

Moreover, the existing results give, for real \(x\),
\[
|F_\lambda(x)-F_{\lambda,N}(x)|
\le
\frac{|x|^{2N}}{(2N)!}\prod_{j=1}^{N}\beta_j.
\]
Combining this with the established coefficient envelope gives
\[
|F_\lambda(x)-F_{\lambda,N}(x)|
\le
\left[
\frac{e|x|\operatorname{arcosh}(2N+10)}{8N}
\right]^{2N}.
\]

Thus, for any fixed \(0<r<1\), we can take
\[
X_N=\frac{8rN}{e\operatorname{arcosh}(2N+10)}
\]
and obtain error at most \(r^{2N}\) throughout \(|x|\le X_N\). The window grows roughly like \(N/\log N\).

**So the increasing-height approximation you describe is already supported by the existing machinery.** That observation gives us something concrete to build on.

Passing a zero statement to the limit is also a sound mathematical mechanism. Suppose we construct entire approximants \(G_N\) such that:

- \(G_N\to H_0\) uniformly on every compact subset of the complex plane;
- every zero of \(G_N\) inside \(|z|<R_N\) is real;
- \(R_N\to\infty\).

Then every zero of \(H_0\) is real. A hypothetical nonreal zero would have a small surrounding disk away from the real axis; convergence forces nearby approximant zeros, contradicting the second condition. This is the standard Hurwitz/Rouché argument. [Topping, §10.2](https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/maths/people/staff/peter_topping/teaching/ma3b8_cplxanal_24_07_29.pdf)

For the theta quadrature approximations, compact complex convergence can also be justified using moment matching and the rapid source decay; I included that argument in the saved note. **The substantial missing ingredient is the finite zero statement.**

Here is why it requires its own argument. For a standard Gaussian source,
\[
F(z)=e^{-z^2/2},
\]
which has no zeros. Its three-position Jacobi approximation is
\[
F_3(z)=\frac23+\frac13\cos(\sqrt3z).
\]
It has nonreal zeros, including
\[
z=\frac{\pi\pm i\operatorname{arcosh}2}{\sqrt3}.
\]
Thus real eigenvalues of \(J_N\), real roots of \(P_N\), and excellent approximation do not automatically give real zeros of the Fourier observation. This example concerns ordinary truncation; it does not rule out a corrected truncation or a theta-specific argument.

I see three further strategies worth exploring alongside the coefficient induction.

1. **Carry an approximation to the entire omitted tail.**  
   This is especially close to your suggestion. Cutting \(J\) disconnects the higher modes. Instead, we can replace them by an effective boundary response describing how they influence the retained modes. That response is a function, rather than a single coefficient. Adding another basis position gives an exact recursive update of the response through a continued fraction. An induction could carry an enclosure of this function and improve it as \(N\) increases. The open question is whether that enclosure can retain enough information about cancellation to control Fourier zeros.

2. **Carry a zero certificate on an expanding region.**  
   Here the inductive hypothesis contains more than “the approximation is accurate.” It includes real-zero brackets, a complete zero count, and error margins on surrounding complex contours. For example, if an approximant has exactly one zero in a disk symmetric about the real axis, and
   \[
   |H_0-G_N|<|G_N|
   \]
   on the disk’s boundary, then \(H_0\) also has exactly one zero there. Conjugation symmetry forces that zero to be real. We must additionally exclude extra zeros elsewhere in the region. The induction would extend the region while preserving these margins. An outer zero count alone would not suffice, because it cannot distinguish two real zeros from a conjugate pair.

3. **Use polynomials constructed to encode the Fourier zero question.**  
   Jensen polynomials are the classical example. They are built from Taylor coefficients of the completed function—hence ultimately from source moments—and are different from the source-orthogonal \(P_n(u)\). Their all-degree real-rootedness is a known RH-equivalent formulation. A new induction proving that property would be substantive; merely translating our coefficients into that formulation would leave the central problem untouched. The relevant induction would increase degree, whereas known eventual-hyperbolicity results fix degree and increase a separate shift parameter. [Griffin–Ono–Rolen–Zagier, pp. 1–2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1902.07321v2)

For your proposed direction, I would initially focus on **what information about the omitted tail must accompany a finite approximation to make its zeros controllable**. That gives the coefficient estimates a specific purpose and helps determine what the inductive hypothesis should contain.

The repository’s weighted-square collision controls are useful here: they satisfy the existing coefficient envelope and approximation properties. A successful zero-preserving step therefore needs an additional estimate that distinguishes the complete theta source. We have not yet identified that estimate.

Exactly—the higher modes matter through excursions that leave the retained part of the chain and return. Their contributions are already inside the amplitude at position zero.

Your other comments suggest a sharper direction: **seek an induction on a controlled description of the omitted tail, with confinement of zeros to a shrinking strip as a consequence.** I would keep this in the chain language and leave the Jensen route aside.

The BBGKY analogy becomes quite concrete once we write the amplitude equations. Freeze \(\lambda\), and put
\[
\psi(x)=e^{ixJ}e_0.
\]
Then
\[
\psi_n'(x)
=i\bigl(a_n\psi_{n-1}(x)+a_{n+1}\psi_{n+1}(x)\bigr),
\qquad
\psi_n(0)=\delta_{n0},
\]
and the desired observation is \(F_\lambda(x)=\psi_0(x)\).

Here \(x\) plays the evolution variable; we are temporarily holding Newman time fixed. If we retain positions \(0,\ldots,N-1\), the last retained equation needs \(\psi_N\). That is the hierarchy-closure problem.

**We can eliminate the omitted amplitudes exactly before making any approximation.** Let \(y(x)\) be the retained vector, and let \(J^{[N]}\) denote the disconnected tail beginning at position \(N\). Define its return amplitude
\[
k_N(t)=\langle e_N,e^{itJ^{[N]}}e_N\rangle.
\]
Solving the omitted equations and substituting back gives
\[
\boxed{
y'(x)=iJ_Ny(x)
-\beta_N e_{N-1}
\int_0^x k_N(x-s)y_{N-1}(s)\,ds.
}
\]

The integral records an amplitude leaving the retained chain at an earlier height \(s\), evolving in the tail, and returning. The factor \(\beta_N=a_N^2\) accounts for crossing the boundary twice.

This equation identifies exactly what we would approximate:

- Ordinary matrix truncation discards the entire memory term.
- A tail closure replaces \(k_N\) by a simpler response and controls the difference.
- A self-consistent closure would determine that response using constraints shared with the retained chain.

This is closely related to the projection-with-memory approach of Mori–Zwanzig. BBGKY supplies the broader analogy of reconstructing higher levels from lower levels while preserving compatibility. Our index measures polynomial degree rather than particle-correlation order, so a particular BBGKY closure cannot simply be imported. [Chorin–Hald–Kupferman, §2](https://math.huji.ac.il/~razk/Publications/PDF/CHK00.pdf), [Akbari et al., §§II.B–C](https://arxiv.org/html/1204.4395v1)

There is also an exact hierarchy **for the tail responses themselves**:
\[
k_n'(x)
=-\beta_{n+1}\int_0^x k_{n+1}(x-s)k_n(s)\,ds,
\qquad k_n(0)=1.
\]
Equivalently, their Laplace transforms satisfy
\[
\widehat k_n(s)
=\frac{1}{s+\beta_{n+1}\widehat k_{n+1}(s)},
\qquad s>0.
\]
Thus we have a precise relation between successive levels on which to study closure. It still contains the deeper response; writing this recurrence does not by itself close the hierarchy.

Your source-dependent identity could help constrain that closure. With the normalized polynomials, it becomes
\[
\langle q_n,V_\lambda' q_{n-1}\rangle_{\mu_\lambda}
=\frac{n}{a_n},
\]
or, in chain notation,
\[
\boxed{a_n[V_\lambda'(J)]_{n,n-1}=n.}
\]

This links the two sides of the problem:

- The memory equation describes **how a tail affects the retained observation**.
- The source identity constrains **which coefficients and tails can belong to the specified source**.

For polynomial \(V'\), the matrix \(V'(J)\) has finite bandwidth, producing relations involving finitely many neighboring coefficients. For the theta source, this matrix function generally involves the whole chain.

There is a useful caution here: replacing \(J\) by \(J_N\) inside \(V'(J)\) also discards tail contributions. A consistent closure would need to account for that correction alongside the correction to the propagator. That is a concrete mathematical connection between your BBGKY suggestion and the integration-by-parts identity.

I would therefore explore **compatibility between the tail approximation and the exact source constraint**, before choosing a mean-field or short-memory ansatz. Large polynomial degree alone has not yet supplied a parameter that makes either approximation controlled.

Your suggestion about zeros approaching the line is sufficient, and it gives us more flexibility than demanding exact reality at every finite stage. Suppose a chosen closure produces entire functions \(G_N\) such that
\[
G_N\longrightarrow F_0
\quad\text{uniformly on every compact complex set},
\]
and
\[
G_N(z)=0,\quad |z|<R_N
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
|\operatorname{Im}z|\le\delta_N,
\]
where \(R_N\to\infty\) and \(\delta_N\to0\).

Then \(F_0\) has only real zeros. Indeed, a hypothetical nonreal zero has a small surrounding disk a positive distance from the real axis. Compact convergence forces approximant zeros into that disk, eventually contradicting the shrinking-strip condition. This uses the same Hurwitz/Rouché mechanism as before. [Topping, §10.2](https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/maths/people/staff/peter_topping/teaching/ma3b8_cplxanal_24_07_29.pdf)

Several features make this useful:

- We need not label corresponding zeros across successive approximations.
- We need not assume that the limiting zeros are simple.
- We can even allow the strip width to depend on a fixed observation window: for each fixed \(R\), a width \(\delta_N(R)\to0\) suffices.

The limiting argument itself needs no quantitative comparison between approximation error and zero spacing. Such comparisons might be needed to establish the finite-stage strip property, depending on the method.

**I would treat shrinking-strip confinement as the desired output of an inductive invariant, rather than immediately making it the whole induction hypothesis.** Merely assuming that confinement holds at degree \(N\) gives little information about why it should hold at degree \(N+1\).

A possible inductive package would carry three kinds of information:

1. **Tail information:** a model for the omitted response and a structured description of its residual.
2. **Source consistency:** constraints showing that this description applies to the actual theta chain.
3. **A preserved structural property:** something that survives moving the cutoff and implies confinement of the scalar observation’s zeros.

The first two now have explicit equations to work with. The third remains unidentified. One possibility is to find a class of boundary responses preserved by the one-site update, then determine whether that class controls the cancellation in the Fourier observation. Another is to find a source identity that controls the residual in a way preserved under refinement.

The existing collision controls tell us that normalization, positivity of the source measure, and generic hierarchy compatibility will not suffice. The distinguishing information must come from stronger consequences of the complete theta source. The displayed source identity is one place to look, although its generic integration-by-parts form alone is shared by other sources.

That gives a structural next question: **what restrictions does the complete theta score impose on the tail response, and which of those restrictions survive the one-site update?** A theorem answering that would advance the induction program. Increasing the cutoff numerically without such a proposed mechanism would not address the issue you want to resolve.

Yes—the key convention is that **turning a ket into its bra takes the adjoint**, which conjugates \(i\). Suppressing \(\lambda\), for real \(t\),
\[
|\psi(t)\rangle=e^{itJ}|e_0\rangle
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\langle\psi(t)|=\langle e_0|e^{-itJ},
\]
because \(J^\dagger=J\).

Consequently, your intended midpoint splitting is
\[
\boxed{
F_\lambda(x)
=\langle\psi(-x/2)\mid\psi(x/2)\rangle
=\langle e_0|e^{ixJ/2}e^{ixJ/2}|e_0\rangle.
}
\]
The operators inside the matrix element have the same sign; the two states described by the inner product have opposite evolution parameters. Using the same state in both slots instead gives its conserved norm, \(1\).

Now inserting the identity really does give a nontrivial sum:
\[
F_\lambda(x)=
\sum_\mu
\langle e_0|e^{ixJ/2}|e_\mu\rangle
\langle e_\mu|e^{ixJ/2}|e_0\rangle.
\]
For our real symmetric Jacobi matrix, writing
\(c_\mu(t)=\langle e_\mu|e^{itJ}|e_0\rangle\), this becomes
\[
\boxed{F_\lambda(x)=\sum_\mu c_\mu(x/2)^2,}
\qquad
\sum_\mu |c_\mu(x/2)|^2=1.
\]
So these are **complex amplitude squares**, not absolute-value squares.

Your midpoint intuition therefore works: truncating this sum retains finitely many intermediate modes. Their amplitudes still depend on the full chain, which is where the omitted-tail approximation enters.
